records.name_note: The three admissible dedicated pages lead with different common names. MoBot's Common Name line gives "European cranberrybush" and its prose says "commonly called European cranberry bush". NC State's page-title parenthetical lists "Cranberry Bush Viburnum, European Cranberry, European Cranberrybush Viburnum, Guelder-Rose" (an alphabetized list, in the same order as its Common Name(s) field; the first entry is Cranberry Bush Viburnum). RHS's subtitle is "guelder rose", with "European cranberry bush" only in its "Other common names" list. European cranberrybush was chosen because it matches MoBot's Common Name line; NC State's nearest entry is "European Cranberrybush Viburnum". NC State also lists Viburnum trilobum under 'Previously known as'; V. trilobum was not researched or merged here. NC State's Description opens with the name 'European cranberry'. The MoBot page was read by the researcher only, with TLS verification switched off; its two quotes cannot be re-checked from this machine. Distinct from the viburnums already in this catalog (Koreanspice Viburnum, Arrowwood Viburnum, Smooth Witherod, Blackhaw Viburnum, Doublefile Viburnum) and from Vaccinium macrocarpon (American Cranberry).
records.toxicity_detail: RHS's Viburnum opulus page, 'Potentially harmful' field: "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Fruit are ornamental; not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". RHS gives no symptoms and no severity rating, and its 'Pets:' line names no animal, so it is neither a cat nor a dog statement. NC State's page for this species carries no Poison block and no Problem for Cats or Problem for Dogs values. The admissible sources disagree directly on eating the fruit, so is_edible is left null. NC State's Edibility field reads "Drupes can be eaten off the bush or used in jams.", and its Description, comparing the species with the native var. americanum, adds "Also, the fruit is more bitter and less desirable for making jellies and sauces." MoBot says "The berries (drupes) are technically edible, but are very bitter in taste and are not recommended for eating fresh off the shrub." RHS says "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten." No admissible page states that the raw fruit causes stomach upset or that it is edible only when cooked.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: RHS's only warning is fruit-scoped and names no cat or dog (its 'Pets:' line names no specific animal); NC State has no Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags for this species, and MoBot has no toxicity statement.

is_edible is null because the admissible sources contradict each other directly: NC State's Edibility field says "Drupes can be eaten off the bush or used in jams."; MoBot (read by the researcher with TLS verification off) says "technically edible, but are very bitter in taste and are not recommended for eating fresh off the shrub"; RHS says "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." This is a source conflict that includes an explicit not-to-be-eaten statement, not a conditional edibility, so neither true nor false is supported (the Flowering Quince precedent from b85). No admissible page states that the raw fruit causes stomach upset or that it is edible only when cooked.

is_houseplant is false: no admissible source addresses indoor culture. NC State's Plant Type field (Perennial, Shrub) and USDA zones 2a-8b describe a hardy outdoor shrub, and its Description places it in hedges and shrub borders.

water_regime left null: MoBot's structured Water field reads 'Medium to wet' (the second-wettest band on MoBot's scale), but that page was read only by the researcher with TLS verification off and cannot be re-checked from this machine, and its culture text ('average, medium moisture' and 'consistent moisture') is a soil preference, not a watering statement; NC State's Moist tag is soil-only. water_dry_down_target and day-interval fields null because no source frames watering that way for an in-ground shrub.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) (open-ended bands), and RHS lists pH as Acid or Alkaline or Neutral.

soil_drainage moderate: NC State tags Good Drainage, Moist and Occasionally Wet; RHS says moist but well-drained or well-drained; MoBot says well-drained with Water Medium to wet. Not fast, since the plant tolerates wet sites.

Mature size: NC State's Dimensions block (12-16 ft tall, 8-15 ft wide) is used. MoBot gives 8-15 ft height and 10-15 ft spread (prose 10-15 ft tall). RHS gives max 4-8 m height and 2.5-4 m spread (UK-calibrated).

RHS lists 'Native to GB/Ireland: Yes' while NC State and MoBot give a European, Asian and North African native range with invasive tendencies in North America; MoBot and NC State both flag it as weedy and potentially invasive, and NC State recommends considering a native alternative.

NC State lists V. trilobum as 'Previously known as' and lists V. opulus 'Roseum' and V. trilobum under 'often confused with'; no V. trilobum or Roseum content is used here. NC State notes the plant resembles the native var. americanum, whose fruit is less bitter.

Temperature, humidity, light in fc, fertilizer, chill damage and pH-range fields are null: no admissible source states them for this species (MoBot Zone 3 to 8 and RHS H6 are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset temperatures).

MoBot's plantfinder.mobot.org page was read by the researcher via curl with certificate verification off (-k) because the local CA chain could not verify the host. verify_quotes cannot reach the host from this machine (ConnectError), so the researcher's MoBot citations stand as read by the researcher and SKIP; no MoBot citation was added at landing. Every value they support (common_name excepted) is also supported by NC State or RHS.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. RHS's page title for this taxon is "Ligustrum vulgare | wild privet" and it lists common privet under "Other common names". NC State's Common Name(s) list on its Ligustrum vulgare page is alphabetized (Amur, Common Privet, Ligustrum, Privet, Wax-leaf), in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, and its description prose calls the plant "Common privet". Common Privet was chosen because it appears on both dedicated pages and is the name NC State's prose uses; the Amur and Wax-leaf entries were not used. Distinct from Ligustrum japonicum (Japanese Privet), already in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Ligustrum vulgare page carries a 'Poisonous to Humans' block: Poison Severity "Medium" (the page banners "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics."); Poison Symptoms "Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, drooling, diarrhea, headache, weakness, low blood pressure, cold and clammy skin possibly lasting 48 to 72 hours, colic, depression."; Poison Toxic Principle "Glycosides: syringin (ligustrin), a glycoside; shikimic acid (lowest toxic dose 4,000mg); saponins, protoanemonin and others"; Causes Contact Dermatitis "No"; Poison Part "Fruits" and "Leaves". Separately from that human-scoped block, NC State's Problems field lists Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses and Weedy; its Plant Type field carries Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub and Weed; and its tag line includes "#poisonous #problem for cats #problem for dogs #problem for horses". The page gives no pet-specific symptom list. RHS's own Ligustrum vulgare page, 'Potentially harmful' field: "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" and "Pets (dogs): Harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". toxic_to_pets is true on NC State's cat- and dog-scoped Problems values, with RHS's dog-scoped line as corroboration. The sources differ in scope: RHS names no plant part, whereas NC State limits the Poison Part to Fruits and Leaves, and RHS's gloves-when-handling warning sits beside NC State's "Causes Contact Dermatitis: No". Neither source gives any preparation or edibility instructions.
unknowns: WEEDY/INVASIVE STATUS: NC State states it 'can be weedy in disturbed areas and has escaped and naturalized in moist areas' and is listed as invasive in North Carolina by the North Carolina Native Plant Society ('Significant Threat'); NC State also says it is 'not recommended for gardens or landscapes' and tags it #aggressive #naturalizes #weedy, with Plant Type including Weed.

Missouri Botanical Garden (plantfinder.mobot.org kempercode=c324) could not be loaded in this session (the www host 301-redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org, which failed with a connect/certificate error), so no MoBot content is used or cited. No Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU or UMD page dedicated to Ligustrum vulgare was found (those are genus-level), so none is cited.
is_houseplant is false: neither admissible page addresses indoor growing. NC State's Plant Type field (Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub, Weed) and USDA zones 4a-7b describe a hardy outdoor shrub.

soil_drainage: moderate is read from NC State's Soil Drainage tags Good Drainage + Moist + Occasionally Dry (spanning occasionally dry and moist) together with its 'good drainage' prose; RHS says only 'Well-drained' for moisture. NC State also lists root rot as a common disease problem. The prose does not say sharp drainage is required. NC State says it "does best in clay, loamy and sandy soils that have good drainage" (Soil Texture: Clay, Loam (Silt), Sand).
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State gives no pH; RHS lists pH as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (no numeric bounds).

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives a watering statement for this plant; NC State's 'Moist' is a soil-drainage tag, and drought tolerance is a trait, not a watering instruction. water_dry_down_target and day-interval fields left null for an in-ground shrub.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's species prose says only that it tolerates full sun or partial shade; its Light values carry their own hour ranges, but the Full sun value ('6 or more hours') is open-ended and gives no ceiling.

mature size: NC State prose (no Dimensions block on this page) gives 'up to 10 to 15 feet tall and spread up to 8 to 15 feet wide' (120-180 in tall, 96-180 in wide, used here). records.name_note: NC State's page-title parenthetical for Cryptomeria japonica reads "Japanese Cedar, Japanese Cryptomeria", and its Common Name(s) list shows the same two names in the same order. RHS's page for this species is titled "Japanese cedar" and lists other common names "Japanese red cedar, sugi". "Japanese cedar" is therefore the name used here. NC State places Japanese cedar in the cypress family (Cupressaceae); the genus is Cryptomeria, not Cedrus. Distinct from Juniperus virginiana (Eastern Redcedar) and Chamaecyparis thyoides (Atlantic White Cedar), already in this catalog.
unknowns: MoBot Plant Finder (kempercode=a158) could not be read: the www.missouribotanicalgarden.org URL redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org, and every fetch failed with a connection or certificate error, so nothing was taken from MoBot.

Clemson HGIC's dedicated page (hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/japanese-cryptomeria/) returned HTTP 403 to the script fetcher. Its content was read only through a summarising fetch, so it is not cited. It uses 'Japanese Cryptomeria' as its H1 and mentions 'Japanese cedar'. The sources therefore split on the primary common name, and the name used here follows NC State and RHS. Clemson's tree-form size range (50-80 ft tall) also runs broader than NC State's.
UF/IFAS has only a cultivar page ('Yoshino', ST219), and PSU, UMD and UGA have no dedicated page for this species, so none of them were used.

is_houseplant is false: no admissible source says it is grown indoors. NC State's Plant Type field (Perennial, Tree) and USDA zones 5a-9b describe an outdoor tree, and NC State recommends it as a specimen tree in a lawn or naturalized area; its Container Gardens landscape link states nothing about indoor culture.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null because no admissible source states any toxicity for this species. is_edible is null because no admissible source addresses eating it (NC State mentions only the wood's use for building). attracts_pollinators is null because no source names pollinators.

water_regime is null. NC State's 'moist' and RHS's 'Moisture: Moist but well-drained' describe soil, not a watering instruction, and no watering statement was found. soil_drainage is set to moderate from NC State's prose 'rich, moist, well-drained' and RHS's 'moist but well-drained', and RHS also warns of Phytophthora root rot. The watering and fertilizing fields are null, as is the dry-down target, because this is an in-ground tree and no source frames care that way.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null. NC State's structured Soil pH is the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band, and RHS lists acid, alkaline and neutral soils as acceptable, so no floor or ceiling can be set.

RHS lists Max Spread 4-8 metres (about 157-315 in) and Max Height 'Higher than 12 metres' (open-ended, so no bound). The sizes used are NC State's structured Dimensions block (50-70 ft tall, 20-30 ft wide). RHS's spread overlaps but does not match it. NC State also gives named-cultivar sizes, which are excluded.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists Dappled Sunlight, Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours); these are mapped to full_sun and part_shade. RHS agrees (full sun, partial shade). Nothing brighter or darker is claimed.

chill damage, temperature ranges, humidity, light in foot-candles, direct-sun hours and fertilizer fields are null because no admissible source states them. NC State's USDA zone list (5a-9b) is a hardiness range, not a damage-onset temperature. RHS's bare H6 is a UK hardiness rating.

records.name_note: Hybrid Witchhazel is the single entry in NC State's Common Name(s) list on its dedicated Hamamelis x intermedia page, the only admissible dedicated page found for this hybrid; the page renders the name with an ASCII x, normalised here to the multiplication sign. NC State describes it as "an artificial hybrid between H. japonica and H. mollis"; neither parent's page was used for any field. The batch was researched under 'Hybrid Witch Hazel' (two words); NC State writes Witchhazel as one word. Distinct from Hamamelis virginiana (Common Witch Hazel), already in this catalog.
unknowns: Only one admissible dedicated page was found for this exact hybrid: NC State Plant Toolbox (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/hamamelis-x-intermedia/). The page title and H1 render the name with an ASCII x ('Hamamelis x intermedia'), normalised here to the multiplication sign. Its Common Name(s) field and title parenthetical both show the single name 'Hybrid Witchhazel'.

Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder lists only named cultivars of Hamamelis x intermedia (Arnold Promise, Allgold, Aphrodite and others) and no species-level page, so it was not used. A cultivar-only page is not admissible for species-level fields. The plantfinder.mobot.org search was reachable only with TLS verification disabled.

No dedicated RHS page for the hybrid was located. The RHS search is JavaScript-rendered, the guessed slug returned 404, and the RHS Hamamelis page found in the cache is a genus-level guide, which is inadmissible. So there is no RHS Name Status, pH or sun cross-check, and scientific_name_accepted rests on the NC State page title alone.
No dedicated page was found at UF/IFAS, Clemson HGIC, Penn State or UMD. The UGA Field Report landscape page is a multi-species page and was not used.

The NC State page has no Poison block, no 'Problem for Cats/Dogs' tags and no 'Attracts' field, and does not address eating. toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail, is_edible and attracts_pollinators are therefore null. The medicinal astringent uses of H. virginiana were deliberately not borrowed.

Soil pH is left null. NC State's only pH value is the open-ended band 'Acid (<6.0)', which gives no floor. Its prose calls for 'moist, fertile, well-drained acidic soil' and its tags include '#acidic soils tolerant', but neither gives a numeric range.

water_regime is left null. The only moisture wording is the soil adjective in 'moist, fertile, well-drained acidic soil' plus the drainage tags, not a watering statement. Drainage is read as moderate from NC State's prose 'moist, fertile, well-drained acidic soil' (the moist-but-well-drained case), consistent with its Soil Drainage field 'Good Drainage' and 'Occasionally Wet'.

outdoor_sun_exposure comes from NC State's structured Light field: 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)'. Partial Shade maps to part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max is left null because the Full sun value is open-ended ('6 or more hours') and gives no ceiling, and the species prose gives no hour figure.
Mature size is NC State's Dimensions block, converted from feet: height 15-20 ft = 180-240 in, width 8-10 ft = 96-120 in. NC State gives no cultivar size in that block.
Cultivar flower colours and sizes (for example Arnold Promise and Jelena) were kept out of species-level fields.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field (Perennial, Shrub, Tree), USDA zones 4a-9b and its shrub-border, hedge, woodland and winter-garden siting describe an outdoor shrub or small tree. No temperature, humidity, indoor light, watering interval, fertilizer or chill-damage evidence exists on the admissible page, so those fields are null. Hardiness zones 4a-9b are a survival range, not a damage-onset temperature.

normalizations: 2026-10-09: b112 landed (branch claude/database-build-goals-e548af) from the post-audit workflow records. Eight home-landscape shrubs, hedges and small trees: European Cranberrybush, Fragrant Mockorange, Japanese Tree Lilac, Common Privet, Oriental Arborvitae, Japanese Cedar, Baby's Breath Spiraea, Hybrid Witchhazel. Auditor-supplied corrected wording used verbatim for the two removed name_notes (European Cranberrybush, Japanese Tree Lilac) and for every CITATION-LEVEL unknowns fix; every substitute quote ground-truthed first against verify_quotes' own fetch+extract path (b112_qc.py). Landing decisions: Viburnum opulus is_edible stays null (NC State 'Drupes can be eaten off the bush or used in jams.' vs RHS 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten.' vs MoBot 'technically edible, but are very bitter'), the disagreement carried in toxicity_detail in the sources' own words; its common_name rests on MoBot's Common Name line, read by the researcher with TLS verification off -- verify_quotes SKIPs plantfinder.mobot.org from this machine (ConnectError), so the researcher's six MoBot quotes stand unchecked and no MoBot citation was added at landing. Common Privet toxicity_detail rewritten to carry NC State's full Poison block verbatim (cited as the page's contiguous label/value run) with the cat- and dog-scoped Problems values and RHS's 'Pets (dogs)' line. Hamamelis × intermedia keeps the hybrid sign; 'Hybrid Witchhazel' is the single entry in NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list on the hybrid's own page. Bare RHS 'Correct' citations dropped where the audit said so (Fragrant Mockorange, Japanese Tree Lilac, Japanese Cedar, Baby's Breath Spiraea), relabelled with CORR elsewhere. NC State label-glued quotes (Plant Type, Soil Drainage, Attracts) trimmed to their values; no 'Woody Plant' Plant Type value was added anywhere. is_houseplant null -> false on all eight, on NC State's exact Plant Type values plus its USDA zone field. RHS genus-level Spiraea Cultivation boilerplate replaced with the species Position and Moisture cards. Researched names title-cased (Japanese cedar -> Japanese Cedar, European cranberrybush -> European Cranberrybush); no common_name collides with a landed record.
